article.overview: A water extraction system is a class of lunar payload that heats, drills or otherwise liberates water or water-bearing volatiles from lunar regolith or buried ice, so that they can be measured or, in principle, used as an in-situ resource. It belongs to the in-situ resource utilisation (ISRU) category because its purpose is to turn local lunar material into a usable resource rather than to carry every consumable from Earth. The published examples read for this article range from a NASA drill-and-analysis package that launched and landed in 2025 (PRIME-1) [1], to an ESA prospecting payload in preparation for flight (PROSPECT) [2], to ground and field demonstrations of heat-based water capture from 2008 to 2009 [3]. There is no single standard design for this payload class.
article.description: A water extraction system is built around a chain of functions. A sampling element, usually a drill or auger, brings regolith or icy material up from below the surface. A containment and heating element, such as a sealed oven, a heated water bed or a microwave source, drives water and other volatiles out of the sample. A capture or analysis element then either traps the released vapour, for example on a water bed or in a cold trap, or passes it to a mass spectrometer that identifies its composition. A control, power and thermal system protects the sample and keeps the hardware within its operating range. Sampling and extraction can be combined in one instrument or split between a drill and a separate laboratory. The distinction between analysis and production matters: an analytical instrument needs to know how much water a sample contained, whereas an ISRU production system must recover water at useful rates and in useful quantities. The sources read for this article describe analytical systems and demonstrations, not an operating production plant.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a water extraction system is to find out whether water or other volatiles are present in lunar material, where they occur, in what form, and whether they can be recovered usefully. Scientific applications include mapping volatile content in polar regolith, distinguishing water from other released gases, and testing extraction methods under real lunar conditions. NASA describes PRIME-1 as a technology demonstration intended to help scientists better understand lunar resources before planned Artemis crewed missions [1]. ESA describes PROSPECT as assessing volatiles in near-surface regolith, including their abundance and origin, and as having an ISRU objective of extracting oxygen and solar-wind-implanted volatiles from lunar minerals [2]. Engineering applications include supplying water for life support, propellant production and other consumables. None of the sources read reports a water extraction system that has supplied such a resource on the Moon.
article.operating_principle: The basic physical principle is heating to release bound or frozen volatiles. Ice sublimates when warmed, and water held in minerals is released at elevated temperature, so the sample is sealed and heated in steps or ramps while the released gases are measured. PROSPECT uses sealed miniaturised ovens heated to about 1000 °C. Its heating is ramped for evolved-gas analysis, stepped for isotopic work, or applied in a single step for ISRU, and the released gases are analysed by ion-trap or magnetic-sector mass spectrometry [2]. For recovery, the Lunar Water Resource Demonstration captured water on water beds and recovered it by heating the beds to 230 °C or higher [3]. PRIME-1 takes a different route: the TRIDENT drill brings material to the surface, and the MSolo mass spectrometer analyses the sample for water and other components [1]. Whichever route is used, the instrument must distinguish water from the other gases that heating releases.
article.scientific_importance: Water is considered important for lunar exploration because it could support human missions and could be converted into oxygen, hydrogen and other products. Whether usable water exists in lunar regolith, and in what form, therefore affects mission design. A water extraction system turns a remote indication of water into a measured quantity in a real sample. Measurements from polar regolith would help constrain how much volatile material is present, how it is bound and how easily it can be released. The sources read for this article do not report a measured lunar-surface water yield from a water extraction system, so the scientific importance of these systems is currently prospective and rests on the demonstrations and planned missions described below.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a water extraction system. The examples below describe three specific systems at different maturity levels: a NASA package that launched and landed in 2025 with only partly reported results, an ESA payload being prepared for flight, and a 2008 to 2009 ground and field demonstration. Their figures describe different designs and must not be compared as if they did.

examples.name: PRIME-1 TRIDENT drill and MSolo mass spectrometer
examples.type: Flown lunar payload (launched and landed 2025; operational outcome only partly reported)
examples.drill_reach: up to about three feet (about 0.9 m) below the surface, per NASA [1]
examples.analysis_instrument: MSolo: commercial off-the-shelf mass spectrometer modified for space use; analyses sample for water and other components [1]
examples.launch: IM-2 mission, launched from NASA Kennedy on 26 February 2025 on the Nova-C lander named Athena [1]
examples.outcome: Lander came to rest on its side about 820 feet from the intended site; NASA page states the drill deployed and some data were received; drilling depth achieved, sample results and water detection not reported in source read [1]
examples.qualification: Flown hardware; technical parameters beyond depth and analysis function not stated in sources read.

examples.name: ESA PROSPECT drill and sealed-oven laboratory
examples.type: Planned flight payload (in preparation; not flown as of source read)
examples.drill_reach: volatile assessment to about 1 m depth [2]; maximum drill depth not stated
examples.sample_volumes: up to 45 mm³ (to ovens) and up to 8 cm³ [2]
examples.oven_heating: sealed miniaturised ovens heated to about 1000 °C; ramped (evolved gas), stepped (isotopic) or single-step (ISRU) [2]
examples.isru_objective: in-situ extraction of oxygen and solar-wind-implanted volatiles from lunar minerals [2]
examples.launch: Being prepared for flight to the lunar south polar region under NASA CLPS; lander not named; launch timing not stated [2]
examples.qualification: Payload mass and power not stated in source read.

examples.name: Lunar Water Resource Demonstration (RESOLVE)
examples.type: Ground and field demonstration (2008 to 2009; not flight-tested)
examples.field_site: Mauna Kea, November 2008; RESOLVE chemical processing system mounted on CMU rover Scarab [3]
examples.water_recovery: water beds heated to 230 °C or higher recover captured water [3]
examples.tephra_water_content_percent: 0.15 to 0.41% (volcanic ash samples; agreed with gas chromatography) [3]
examples.hydrogen_data: Pure hydrogen, not regolith: over 90% captured; 98% of absorbed hydrogen recovered by heating hydride to 400 °C [3]
examples.qualification: Ground and field testing only; tephra samples, not stated to be lunar simulants [3].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Not published in the sources read for the TRIDENT drill or the MSolo instrument. PROSPECT sample volumes (up to 45 mm³ and 8 cm³) are sample sizes, not instrument dimensions [2]. Specific payload dimensions must be taken from verified mission documentation.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Not stated in the sources read for PRIME-1 or PROSPECT. Mass determines launch and lander requirements, so this gap matters for any compatibility assessment.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not stated in the sources read for PRIME-1 or PROSPECT. The LWRD work did not report power for the field hardware in the source read [3].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A water extraction system must work in vacuum, through large temperature swings, and in abrasive dust. It must also control the sample's thermal history so that volatiles are not lost before measurement. Sealing and thermal control of samples are design drivers for analytical systems, because the stability of volatiles depends on temperature and on the material's grain size and structure. The sources read do not quantify these effects for a specific system. Drills and heating hardware also need power, thermal control and data links from a lander or rover, and the required values are not stated in the sources read.
article.limitations: Heating releases a mixture of gases rather than water alone, so the instrument must identify water among other volatiles; MSolo is described as analysing samples for water and other components [1]. A single sample or borehole may not represent the surrounding regolith. The drilling and water-detection results of PRIME-1 are not reported in the sources read. The demonstrations in [3] used volcanic material under field conditions, and PROSPECT's ISRU objective is oxygen extraction from minerals, which is not the same as water recovery [2]. The sources read do not show a complete extraction-and-recovery chain operating on the Moon.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A water extraction system can reach the Moon as a dedicated payload or as one part of a lander or rover science package. Its drill, heating and analysis hardware must be integrated, launched, landed and deployed, and its sample handling must survive that sequence.
transportation_process: Integrate the drill, heating or analysis hardware with a lander or rover on Earth.
Launch on a launch vehicle and transfer to the Moon. PRIME-1 flew this way on the IM-2 mission, launched from NASA Kennedy on 26 February 2025 [1].
Land and deploy the drill. NASA's PRIME-1 page reports that the drill deployed [1].
Move samples to the extraction or analysis hardware. PROSPECT is described as sending samples to sealed ovens [2]; its transfer mechanism is not described in the source read.
Provide power, thermal control and data relay through the lander or rover.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: For PRIME-1 the drill was carried on the lander and deployed on the lunar surface; the deployment mechanism is not described in the source read [1]. PROSPECT's drill is described as reaching about 1 m [2], with the deployment method not stated.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: PRIME-1 flew on the IM-2 mission [1]. The LWRD and RESOLVE work was a ground and field demonstration [3]. PROSPECT is a planned flight payload [2].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a specific lander or rover is asserted. PRIME-1 flew on the IM-2 Nova-C lander named Athena [1], but the interface data needed to assess other landers are not in the sources read. The IM-2 lander came to rest on its side [1], which illustrates that landing attitude is a serious risk for surface hardware.

article.historical_significance: NASA describes PRIME-1 as a technology demonstration for lunar resources ahead of planned Artemis missions [1]. The LWRD work demonstrated, in a 2008 field test, that water could be captured and recovered by heating water beds [3]. PROSPECT is a planned flight payload that combines drilling, sealed-oven heating and an ISRU objective [2]. Together these examples show how water extraction has moved from ground demonstration toward flight hardware, while the sources read do not yet show a flight result that quantifies water recovered from the Moon.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The name "water extraction system" describes a class of hardware. The examples above differ in purpose, maturity and reported data, so their figures are not interchangeable. Values for drill depth, mass, power and water yield are reported only where a cited source states them. PRIME-1 operational details beyond the NASA page, the TRIDENT and MSolo technical parameters and PROSPECT's flight timing were not verified, because the relevant technical documents could not be read with the available tools. Search results also pointed to a 2026 thermal water-extraction ground test (LUWEX) that could not be read in full, so it is not used here. Some search results gave different mission-duration figures for the IM-2 mission; these were not adopted.
